¶
'''attendress†''' (ạ-ten′dres), ''n.'' [< ''attender'' + ''-ess.''] A female attendant. ''Fuller.''

'''attent†''' (ạ-tent′), ''v. t.'' [A later form of ''attempt'', after the orig. L. ''attentare:'' see ''attempt.''] To attempt. ''Quarles.''

'''attent†''' (ạ-tent′), ''a.'' and ''n.'' [< L. ''attentus'', pp. of ''attendere'', attend: see ''attend.''] '''I.''' ''a.'' Attentive; intent: as, “an ''attent'' ear,” ''Shak.'', Hamlet, i. 2.
{{smaller block|Let thine ears be ''attent.''{{right|2 Chron. vi. 40.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Whylest thus he talkt, the knight with greedy eare
Hong still upon his melting mouth ''attent.''</poem>{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., VI. ix. 26.}}}}

'''II.''' ''n.'' [< ME. ''attente'', ''atente'', < OF. ''atente'', mod. F. ''attente'' = Pr. ''atenta'', prop. pp., < L. ''attenta'', fem. of ''attentus'', pp. of ''attendere:'' see ''attend.''] Attention.
{{smaller block|<poem>So being clad unto the fields he went
With the faire Pastorella every day,
And kept her sheepe with dilligent ''attent.''</poem>{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., VI. ix. 37.}}}}

{{smaller block|<poem>Let ballad-rhymers tire their gallèd wits,

{{right|''Ford'', Fame’s Memorial.}}}}

'''attenuant''' (a̤-ten′ū-ạnt), ''a.'' and ''n.'' [= F. ''atténuant'', < L. ''attenuan(t-)s'', ppr. of ''attenuare'', make thin: see ''attenuate''.] '''I.''' ''a.'' Attenuating; making thin, as fluids; diluting; rendering less dense and viscid.
{{smaller block|Things that be ''attenuant''.
{{right|''Holland'', tr. of Plutarch, p. 642.}}}}

'''II.''' ''n.'' A medicine which increases the fluidity of the humors; a diluent.

'''attenuate''' (a̤-ten′ū-āt), ''v.''; pret. and pp. ''attenuated'', ppr. ''attenuating''. [< L. ''attenuatus'', pp. of ''attenuare'' (> It. ''attenuare'' = Pg. ''attenuar'' = Sp. Pr. ''atenuar'' = F. ''atténuer''), make thin, weaken, lessen, < ''ad'', to, + ''tenuare'', make thin, < ''tenuis'', thin, = E. ''thin'', q. v.] '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To make thin or slender; reduce in thickness; wear or draw down: as, an ''attenuated'' thread or wire.
readings.c3s3:
state of being thin or thinned; diminution of density or viscidity: as, the ''attenuation'' of the humors; specifically, in ''brewing'' and ''distilling'', the thinning or clarifying of saccharine worts by the conversion of the sugar into alcohol and carbonic acid.

{{smaller block|The decrease in density [of the beer-worts] is called ''attenuation.''
{{right|''Thausing'', Beer (trans.), p. 707.}}}}

'''atter'''<sup>1</sup>† (at′ėr), ''n.'' [< ME. ''atter'', < AS. ''āttor'', ''ǣttor'', more correctly ''ātor'', ''āter'', poison, = OS. ''ētar'', ''ēttar'' = D. ''etter'' = OHG. ''eitar'', ''eitter'', MHG. G. ''eiter'', poison, pus, = Icel. ''eitr'' = Sw. ''etter'' = Dan. ''edder'', ''œdder'', poison, connected with OHG. MHG. ''eiz'', a boil, sore; cf. Gr. οἶδος, οἶδμα, a tumor, swelling: see ''œdema''.] Poison; venom; pus. ''Holland.''

'''atter'''<sup>2</sup>† (a-tėr′), ''v. t.'' [< F. ''atterrer'', < ML. ''atterrare'', prostrate, cast down, carry earth from one place to another, < L. ''ad'', to, + ''terra'', earth. Cf. ''inter''.] To place upon or in the earth; cast down to the earth; humble; subdue. Also written ''atterr''.

{{smaller block|''Atterrs'' the stubborn and attracts the prone.
{{right|''Sylvester'', tr. of Du Bartas.}}}}

<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|attendance|372|atter}}</noinclude>—To dance attendance. See ''dance''.

'''attendancy†''' (a-ten′dan-si), ''n.'' '''1.''' Attendance; a train or retinue.   ''Fuller.''
{{smaller block|Of honour another part is ''attendancy''; and therefore, in the visions of the glory of God, angels are spoken of as his attendants. . . . It sheweth what honour is fit for prelates, and what ''attendancy''.
{{right|''Hooker'', Eccles. Pol., vii. § 20 (Ord MS.).}}}}
'''2.''' Relation; relative position.
{{smaller block|To name lands by the ''attendancy'' they have to other lands more notorious.
{{right|''Bacon'', Maxims of the Law, xxiv.}}}}

'''attendant''' (a-ten′dant), ''a.'' and ''n.''   [< F. ''attendant'' (= It. ''attendente''), ppr. of ''attendre'', wait: see ''attend'' and ''-ant''<sup>1</sup>.]   '''I.''' ''a.'' '''1.''' Accompanying; being present or in attendance.
{{smaller block|<poem>Other suns perhaps,
With their ''attendant'' moons, thou wilt descry.</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', P. L., viii. 149.}}}}
'''2.''' Accompanying, connected, or immediately following as consequential: as, intemperance, with all its ''attendant'' evils.
{{smaller block|Those bodily pains and sufferings which . . . are but too frequently ''attendant'' upon any disorder of the fancy.
{{right|''Barham'', Ingoldsby Legends, I. 183.}}}}
'''3†.''' In ''law'', depending on or connected with something or some person; owing duty or service.{{smaller|—'''Attendant keys''', in ''music'', same as ''relative keys''. See ''relative''.}}

'''II.''' ''n.'' '''1.''' One who attends or accompanies another, in any character; especially, one who belongs to a train or retinue; a follower.
{{smaller block|Brave ''attendants'' near him.
{{right|''Shak.'', T. of the S., Ind., i.}}}}
{{smaller block|The Furies, they said, are ''attendants'' on justice, and if the sun in heaven should transgress his path, they would punish him.
{{right|''Emerson'', Compensation.}}}}

'''2.''' One who attends on or waits the pleasure of another, as a suitor or the like.
{{smaller block|To give an ''attendant'' quick despatch is a civility.
{{right|''T. Burnet'', Theory of the Earth.}}}}
Specifically—'''3.''' In ''law'', one who owes a duty or service to, or depends on, another.—'''4.''' One who is present, as at a public meeting, for any purpose.
{{smaller block|He was a constant ''attendant'' at all meetings relating to charity.
{{right|''Swift.''}}}}
'''5.''' That which accompanies or is consequent on anything.
{{smaller block|He that early arriveth unto the parts and prudence of age, is happily old without the uncomfortable ''attendants'' of it.
{{right|''Sir T. Browne'', Letter to a Friend.}}}}
{{smaller block|An extreme jealousy of power is the ''attendant'' on all popular revolutions, and has seldom been without its evils.
{{right|''A. Hamilton'', Continentalist, No. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|'''Master attendant''', an officer of an English dockyard, generally a staff commander, whose duty it is to inspect moorings, move and secure vessels, care for ships in ordinary, and generally to assist the superintendent. ='''Syn. 1.''' Associate, escort, retainer.—'''5.''' Accompaniment, concomitant.}}

'''attender''' (a̤-ten′dėr), ''n.'' '''1.''' One who attends or gives heed.
{{smaller block|Attending to conduct, to judgment, makes the ''attender'' feel that it is joy to do it.
{{right|''M. Arnold'', Literature and Dogma, i.}}}}
'''2.''' An attendant; a companion.

'''attendingly''' (a̤-ten′ding-li), ''adv.'' With attention; attentively.

'''attendment†''' (a̤-tend′ment), ''n.''   [< ''attend'' + ''-ment.'']   An accompanying circumstance: as, “uncomfortable ''attendments'' of hell,” ''Sir T. Browne'', Vulg. Err., vii. 16.

'''attendress†''' (ạ-ten′dres), ''n.''   [< ''attender'' + ''-ess.'']   A female attendant.   ''Fuller.''

'''attent†''' (ạ-tent′), ''v. t.''   [A later form of ''attempt'', after the orig. L. ''attentare:'' see ''attempt.'']   To attempt.   ''Quarles.''

'''attent†''' (ạ-tent′), ''a.'' and ''n.''   [< L. ''attentus'', pp. of ''attendere'', attend: see ''attend.'']   '''I.''' ''a.'' Attentive; intent: as, “an ''attent'' ear,” ''Shak.'', Hamlet, i. 2.
{{smaller block|Let thine ears be ''attent.''{{right|2 Chron. vi. 40.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Whylest thus he talkt, the knight with greedy eare
Hong still upon his melting mouth ''attent.''</poem>{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., VI. ix. 26.}}}}

'''II.''' ''n.'' [< ME. ''attente'', ''atente'', < OF. ''atente'', mod. F. ''attente'' = Pr. ''atenta'', prop. pp., < L. ''attenta'', fem. of ''attentus'', pp. of ''attendere:'' see ''attend.''] Attention.
{{smaller block|<poem>So being clad unto the fields he went
With the faire Pastorella every day,
And kept her sheepe with dilligent ''attent.''</poem>{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., VI. ix. 37.}}}} thing done after an extra-judicial appeal. (''c'') A matter improperly innovated or attempted by an inferior judge.

'''attention''' (a-ten′sho̤n), ''n.''   [< ME. ''attencioun'' (F. ''attention''), < L. ''attentio''(''n''-), < ''attendere'', pp. ''attentus'', attend, give heed to: see ''attend''.]   '''1.''' Active direction of the mind upon an object of sense or of thought, giving it relative or absolute prominence: it may be either voluntary or involuntary.
{{smaller block|When the ideas that offer themselves are taken notice of, and, as it were, registered in the memory, it is ''attention.'' {{right|''Locke'', Human Understanding, ii. 19.}}}}
{{smaller block|In the relation of events, and the delineation of characters, they have paid little ''attention'' to facts, to the costume of the times of which they pretend to treat, or to the general principles of human nature. {{right|''Macaulay'', On History.}}}}
{{smaller block|A trained pianist will play a new piece of music at sight, and perhaps have so much ''attention'' to spare that he can talk with you at the same time. {{right|''J. Fiske'', Evolutionist, p. 308.}}}}
'''2.''' The power or faculty of mental concentration.
{{smaller block|In the childhood of our race and of each one of us, the ''attention'' was called forth by the actions upon us of external nature. {{right|''Mivart'', Nature and Thought, p. 18.}}}}
'''3.''' Consideration; observant care; notice: as, your letter has just arrived, and will receive early ''attention.''—'''4.''' Civility or courtesy, or an act of civility or courtesy: as, ''attention'' to a stranger; in the plural, acts of courtesy indicating regard: as, his ''attentions'' to the lady were most marked.—'''5.''' In ''milit. tactics'', a cautionary word used as a preparative to a command to execute some manœuver: as, ''attention'', company! right face! {{smaller|='''Syn. 1.''' Notice, heed, mindfulness, observance; study.—'''4.''' Politeness, deference.}}

'''attentive''' (ạ-ten′tiv), ''a.''   [< F. ''attentif'', < L. as if *''attentivus'', < ''attendere'', pp. ''attentus'', attend: see ''attend'', ''attent'', and ''-ive''.]   '''1.''' Characterized by or of the nature of attention; heedful; intent; observant; regarding with care; mindful: as, an ''attentive'' ear or eye; an ''attentive'' listener; an ''attentive'' act.
{{smaller block|<poem>Like Cato, give his little senate laws,
And sit ''attentive'' to his own applause.</poem>
{{right|''Pope'', Prol. to Satires, l. 210.}}}}
{{smaller block|They know the King to have been always their most ''attentive'' scholar and imitator. {{right|''Milton'', Eikonoklastes, xxiv.}}}}
'''2.''' Characterized by consideration or observant care; assiduous in ministering to the comfort or pleasure of others; polite; courteous: as, ''attentive'' to the ladies.
{{smaller block|Herbert proved one of the most ''attentive'' guards on the line. {{right|''G. A. Sala.''}}}}
{{smaller|='''Syn.''' Regardful, watchful, circumspect, wary, careful, thoughtful, alert.}}

'''attentively''' (ạ-ten′tiv-li), ''adv.''   [< ''attentive'' + ''-ly''<sup>2</sup>; ME. ''attentifly'' (Wyclif).]   In an attentive manner; heedfully; carefully; with fixed attention.

'''attentiveness''' (ạ-ten′tiv-nes), ''n.'' The state of being attentive; heedfulness; attention.

'''attently†''' (ạ-tent′li), ''adv.'' Attentively.   ''Barrow.''

'''attentor†''' (ạ-ten′tor), ''n.''   [< L. as if *''attentor'' (cf. ML. ''attensor'', an observer), < ''attendere'', pp. ''attentus'', attend.]   A listener.
<poem>Let ballad-rhymers tire their gallèd wits,
Scorns to their patrons, making juiceless mirth
To gross ''attentors'' by their hirèd writs.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Ford'', Fame’s Memorial.}}}}

'''attenuant''' (a̤-ten′ū-ạnt), ''a.'' and ''n.''   [= F. ''atténuant'', < L. ''attenuan(t-)s'', ppr. of ''attenuare'', make thin: see ''attenuate''.]   '''I.''' ''a.'' Attenuating; making thin, as fluids; diluting; rendering less dense and viscid.
{{smaller block|Things that be ''attenuant''.
{{right|''Holland'', tr. of Plutarch, p. 642.}}}}

'''II.''' ''n.'' A medicine which increases the fluidity of the humors; a diluent.

'''attenuate''' (a̤-ten′ū-āt), ''v.''; pret. and pp. ''attenuated'', ppr. ''attenuating''.   [< L. ''attenuatus'', pp. of ''attenuare'' (> It. ''attenuare'' = Pg. ''attenuar'' = Sp. Pr. ''atenuar'' = F. ''atténuer''), make thin, weaken, lessen, < ''ad'', to, + ''tenuare'', make thin, < ''tenuis'', thin, = E. ''thin'', q. v.]   '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To make thin or slender; reduce in thickness; wear or draw down: as, an ''attenuated'' thread or wire. {{smaller block|The earliest conception of a soul is that of an ''attenuated'' duplicate of the body, capable of detachment from the body, yet generally resident in it.
{{right|''Trans. Amer. Philol. Ass.'', XV. 37.}}}}
{{smaller block|The finer part belonging to the juice of grapes, being ''attenuated'' and subtilized, was changed into an ardent spirit.
{{right|''Boyle.''}}}}
'''4.''' To lessen in complexity or intensity; reduce in strength or energy; simplify; weaken: as, the ''attenuated'' remedies of the homeopathists.
{{smaller block|To undersell our rivals . . . has led the manufacturer to ''attenuate'' his processes, in the allotment of tasks, to an extreme point.
{{right|''Is. Taylor.''}}}}
{{smaller block|If correctly reported, Pasteur is convinced that he has discovered means by which the virus of hydrophobia can be ''attenuated'', and that, by the inoculation of the ''attenuated'' virus, individuals may be rendered, for the time being, insusceptible to the disease.
{{right|''Science'', VI. 399.}}}}
'''5.''' Figuratively, to weaken or reduce in force, effect, or value; render meager or jejune; fine down.
{{smaller block|We may reject and reject till we ''attenuate'' history into sapless meagreness.
{{right|''Sir F. Palgrave'', Eng. and Normandy, I. 533.}}}}
{{smaller block|Men of taste are so often ''attenuated'' by their refinements, and dwarfed by the overgrown accuracy and polish of their attainments.
{{right|''Bushnell'', Sermons for New Life, p. 181.}}}}
{{smaller block|Mentschikof tried to ''attenuate'' the extent and effect of his demands.
{{right|''Kinglake.''}}}}
'''6†.''' To lessen; diminish: said of number.   ''Howell.''

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' '''1.''' To become thin, slender, or fine; diminish; lessen. {{smaller block|The attention ''attenuates'' as its sphere contracts.
{{right|''Coleridge.''}}}}
'''2.''' In ''brewing'' and ''distilling'', to undergo the process of attenuation. See ''attenuation'', 4.

'''attenuate''' (a̤-ten′ū-āt), ''a.''   [< L. ''attenuatus'', pp.: see the verb.]   '''1.''' Slender; thin.—'''2.''' In ''bot.'', tapering gradually to a narrow extremity.—'''3.''' Of thin consistency; dilute; rarefied.
{{smaller block|Spirits ''attenuate'', which the cold doth congeal and coagulate.
{{right|''Bacon.''}}}}
{{smaller block|A series of captivating bubbles, each more airy and evanescent, each more ''attenuate'' and fantastic, than its glittering brother.
{{right|''H. James'', Subs. and Shad., p. 345.}}}}

'''attenuation''' (a̤-ten-ụ̄-ā′sho̤n), ''n.''   [< L. ''attenuatio(n-)'', < ''attenuare'': see ''attenuate'', ''v.'']   '''1.''' The act or process of making slender, thin, or lean; the state of being thin; emaciation; reduced thickness or proportions.
{{smaller block|Age had worn to the extreme of ''attenuation'' a face that must always have been hard-featured.
{{right|''R. T. Cooke'', Somebody’s Neighbors, p. 26.}}}}
'''2.''' The act of making fine by comminution or attrition.
{{smaller block|The action of the air facilitates the ''attenuation'' of these rocks.
{{right|''Chaptal'' (trans.), 1791.}}}}
'''3.''' The act or process of lessening in complexity or intensity; reduction of force, strength, or energy; specifically, in ''homeopathy'', the reduction of the active principle of medicines to minute or infinitesimal doses.—'''4.''' The act of making thin or thinner, as a fluid, or the state of being thin or thinned; diminution of density or viscidity: as, the ''attenuation'' of the humors; specifically, in ''brewing'' and ''distilling'', the thinning or clarifying of saccharine worts by the conversion of the sugar into alcohol and carbonic acid.

{{smaller block|The decrease in density [of the beer-worts] is called ''attenuation.''
{{right|''Thausing'', Beer (trans.), p. 707.}}}}

'''atter'''<sup>1</sup>† (at′ėr), ''n.''   [< ME. ''atter'', < AS. ''āttor'', ''ǣttor'', more correctly ''ātor'', ''āter'', poison, = OS. ''ētar'', ''ēttar'' = D. ''etter'' = OHG. ''eitar'', ''eitter'', MHG. G. ''eiter'', poison, pus, = Icel. ''eitr'' = Sw. ''etter'' = Dan. ''edder'', ''œdder'', poison, connected with OHG. MHG. ''eiz'', a boil, sore; cf. Gr. οἶδος, οἶδμα, a tumor, swelling: see ''œdema''.]   Poison; venom; pus.   ''Holland.''

'''atter'''<sup>2</sup>† (a-tėr′), ''v. t.''   [< F. ''atterrer'', < ML. ''atterrare'', prostrate, cast down, carry earth from one place to another, < L. ''ad'', to, + ''terra'', earth. Cf. ''inter''.]   To place upon or in the earth; cast down to the earth; humble; subdue. Also written ''atterr''.

{{smaller block|''Atterrs'' the stubborn and attracts the prone.
{{right|''Sylvester'', tr. of Du Bartas.}}}}<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
